'''Isabel Joy Bear''' {{Post-nominals|country=AUS|AM}} (4 January 1927 – 8 April 2021)<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=http://www.eoas.info/biogs/P004169b.htm|title=Bear, Isabel Joy - Biographical entry - Encyclopedia of Australian Science|last=Centre|first=The University of Melbourne eScholarship Research|website=www.eoas.info|language=en-gb|access-date=11 February 2020}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Isabel Joy BEAR {{!}} Death Notices {{!}} Melbourne|url=https://www.mytributes.com.au/notice/death-notices/isabel-joy-bear/5681184/|access-date=2021-04-12|website=The Cairns Post|language=en}}</ref>  was an Australian chemist who worked at [[CSIRO]] for over forty years. She was the first woman to be awarded the [[Royal Australian Chemical Institute]] Leighton Medal. She was inducted into the [[Victorian Honour Roll of Women]] in 2005. Bear identified several metastable [[zirconium]] sulphate hydrates, and with [[Richard Grenfell Thomas|Dick Thomas]] was the first to scientifically describe "[[petrichor]]", the smell of rain on dry soil.

== Early life and education ==
Bear was born in [[Camperdown, Victoria]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite news|url=https://csiropedia.csiro.au/bear-isabel-joy/|title=Isabel 'Joy' Bear|date=13 January 2015|website=CSIROpedia|language=en-AU|access-date=11 February 2020 |last1=Ward |first1=Colin }}</ref> Her parents were Isabel Hilda Bear and Rolfe William Bear.<ref name=":1" /> Her father had served in the [[Australian Defence Force]], and bought a dairy farm in [[Derrinallum]] after returning from [[World War I]].<ref name=":1" /> She attended the Derrinallum and South Caulfield State Schools and Hampton High School, where she was the school prefect.<ref name=":1" /> Toward the end of her school career, Bear had become interested in scientific research.<ref name=":1" /> In 1944, at only seventeen years old, Bear joined a chemistry laboratory in the first iteration of [[CSIRO]], where she worked as a laboratory assistant.<ref name=":1" /> During the evening she attended the [[Melbourne Technical College]] (now [[RMIT University]]), where she earned diplomas in applied chemistry and applied science.<ref name=":1" /> During the six years it took Bear to complete her diplomas the criteria for joining CSIRO as a researcher had changed, and Bear was no longer eligible to join.<ref name=":1" /> 

== Research and career ==
In the 1950s Bear moved to the [[United Kingdom]], where she worked at the [[Harwell Science and Innovation Campus]].<ref name=":1" /> She moved to the [[University of Birmingham]], where she worked as a postdoctoral researcher in the department of [[metallurgy]].<ref name=":1" /> Whilst working in Birmingham Bear became interested in [[solid-state chemistry]].<ref name=":1" />

Bear joined the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research ([[CSIRO]]) in 1953, where she would go on to work for over forty years.<ref name=":1" /> She specialised in mineral chemistry, studying the chemical properties of [[zirconium]], [[hafnium]] and [[Sulfide|sulphides]].<ref name=":1" /> With Principal Research Scientist [[Frederick Kenneth McTaggart|Ken McTaggart]], Bear studied phototropic effects in white oxides, including [[titanium oxide]].<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=McTaggart|first1=F. K.|last2=Bear|first2=Joy|date=1955|title=Phototropic effects in oxides. I. Titanium dioxide|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/jctb.5010051203|journal=Journal of Applied Chemistry|language=en|volume=5|issue=12|pages=643–653|doi=10.1002/jctb.5010051203|issn=1934-998X|url-access=subscription}}</ref> She worked with the [[Western Mining Co., Ltd.]], with whom she extracted [[lithium]] from [[Western Australia|Western Australian]] [[spodumene]].<ref name=":1" /> In the 1960s Bear identified several new metastable zirconium sulphate hydrates (a [[heptahydrate]] and [[pentahydrate]]) and worked to uncover their crystal structures.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=https://nla.gov.au/nla.party-1475847|title=Bear, Isabel Joy, (AM, FRACI) (1927-) - People and organisations|website=Trove|language=en|access-date=11 February 2020}}</ref> 

In 1964 Bear and her colleague [[Richard Grenfell Thomas|Dick Thomas]] became the first to scientifically describe the smell of rain, for which Thomas coined the term [[petrichor]].<ref>{{Cite news|last=Phillips|first=Angie|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-northern-ireland-49092119|title=The sweet smell of a summer shower?|date=29 July 2019|work=BBC News|access-date=11 February 2020|language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Bear|first1=I. J.|last2=Thomas|first2=R. G.|date=1964|title=Nature of Argillaceous Odour|url=https://www.nature.com/articles/201993a0|journal=Nature|language=en|volume=201|issue=4923|pages=993–995|doi=10.1038/201993a0|bibcode=1964Natur.201..993B |s2cid=4189441 |issn=1476-4687|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Thomas and Bear, like many researchers before them, noticed that dry clays and soils evolve a characteristic odour when they were breathed upon. She performed a series of experiments; steam distilling rocks that had been exposed to dry conditions. During these investigations Bear noticed that the smell was due to a yellowish oil, which they named "petrichor" – blood of the stone.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|url=http://theconversation.com/the-smell-of-rain-how-csiro-invented-a-new-word-39231|title=The smell of rain: how CSIRO invented a new word|last=Poynton|first=Howard|website=The Conversation|date=31 March 2015 |language=en|access-date=11 February 2020}}</ref> In 2015 researchers at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] released a high speed video that visualised the aerosols released during rainfall.<ref>{{Citation|title=Rainfall can release aerosols, high-speed video shows| date=14 January 2015 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Waqmq_GTyjA|language=en|access-date=11 February 2020}}</ref>

In 1967 Bear was promoted to the research staff in the Division of Mineral Chemistry at CSIRO, and was the first and only woman to hold such a position.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /> Bear was eventually awarded a doctoral degree in [[Applied science|Applied Science]] from the Victoria Institute of Colleges in 1978.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /> That year she was promoted to senior principal scientist.<ref name=":2" /> She developed powder anodes from [[galena]] for using in [[electrowinning]] of lead and developed new processes to treat [[lead sulphate]] residues.<ref name=":1" /> 

In 1988 Bear became the first woman to be awarded the [[Royal Australian Chemical Institute]] Leighton Memorial Medal.<ref name=":2" /> She worked to document the history of the CSIRO Division of [[Chemical engineering|Chemical Engineering]] and Australia's heritage in mineral chemistry in ''The History of the CSIRO Division of Mineral Chemistry''.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Bear|first1=IJ|last2=Biegler|first2=T|last3=Scott|first3=TR|date=2001|title=Alumina to Zirconia|url=https://ebooks.publish.csiro.au/content/alumina-zirconia|publisher=CSIRO Publishing|language=en|doi=10.1071/9780643104884|isbn=9780643104884 }}</ref>

Bear retired from the CSIRO in 2015 after a career of more than 70 years.<ref name=":3" />

== Awards and honours ==
* 1974 Elected Fellow of the [[Australasian Institute of Mining and Metallurgy]]<ref name=":0" />
* 1986 Elected Fellow of the [[Royal Australian Chemical Institute]]<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.eoas.info/biogs/A000234b.htm|title=Royal Australian Chemical Institute (RACI) - Corporate entry - Encyclopedia of Australian Science|last=Centre|first=The University of Melbourne eScholarship Research|website=www.eoas.info|language=en-gb|access-date=11 February 2020}}</ref>
* 1986 [[Member of the Order of Australia]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://blog.csiro.au/the-smell-of-rain-how-our-scientists-invented-a-new-word/|title=The smell of rain: how our scientists invented a new word|date=31 March 2015|website=CSIROscope|language=en-AU|access-date=11 February 2020}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://honours.pmc.gov.au/honours/awards/886092|title=Australia Day 1986 Honours List|date=26 January 1986|website=Honours PMC|access-date=11 February 2020}}</ref>
* 1988 Royal Australian Chemical Institute Leighton Memorial Medal<ref name=":0" />
* 2005 [[Victorian Honour Roll of Women]]<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://herplacemuseum.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/03/2005-Honour-Roll-Booklet-1.pdf|title=Victorian Honour Roll of Women|website=Her Place Museum|access-date=11 February 2020}}</ref>
